The BrowseComp† benchmark is a non-standard 150-question subset selected by whether o3 can solve it with web search in five minutes. This selection procedure may bias the benchmark and weakens claims of state-of-the-art performance on BrowseComp.

Reproducibility is limited because the system depends on live web search, Google People Also Ask, Jina API results, and external LLM summarization/judging. There is little discussion of temporal drift, cached retrieval corpora, released data, or variance across runs.

The synthetic HDS-QA construction is narrow and only weakly validated: 2,111 trajectories come from 773 successful questions, generated and filtered automatically, and the authors explicitly retain trajectories with incorrect intermediate steps. Human validation or quality audits are missing.

Accuracy relies heavily on LLM-as-judge evaluation with Qwen3-32B, which is also part of the pipeline, and the paper provides no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or detailed judge calibration.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence, especially “true test-time search scaling” and “state-of-the-art,” given the confounded baselines, curated benchmarks, and missing comparisons to some planning/decomposition search systems under matched retrieval and model conditions.
